title: Determinants measure collapse
learningObjective: Interpret determinants as signed volume scaling and an invertibility test.

retrieve.bodyMarkdown: When does a square linear map have zero kernel? What happens geometrically when independent directions become dependent?

encounter.bodyMarkdown: A shear tilts a square without changing its area. A projection flattens it to a line. A determinant distinguishes these effects with one number.

explain.bodyMarkdown: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, $\det A=ad-bc$. Its absolute value is the area scale; its sign records orientation. In dimension $n$, the determinant is the signed volume scale, normalized to one at the identity, multilinear and alternating in the columns. Dependent columns give zero. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Determinants multiply under composition: $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$. Similar matrices have the same determinant because the factors from $P$ and $P^{-1}$ cancel.

figure.caption: det A = ad − bc = (3)(4) − (1)(2) = 10, the factor by which A scales area.

reflect.bodyMarkdown: A determinant is defined for square matrices. Zero means volume collapse, not necessarily that the map sends every vector to zero.

problems.promptMarkdown: What is the determinant of the shear $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$?

hints.bodyMarkdown: Apply the two-by-two determinant formula.
Subtract the off-diagonal product from the diagonal product.
The off-diagonal product has a zero factor.
The formula gives $1\cdot1-3\cdot0=1$. This shear preserves area and orientation.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The formula gives $1\cdot1-3\cdot0=1$. This shear preserves area and orientation.

problems.promptMarkdown: A real square matrix has determinant zero. What must be true?

options.label: It reverses orientation without changing volume.
options.accessibleLabel: It reverses orientation without changing volume.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Interpret zero as collapse of full-dimensional volume.
Invertibility is equivalent to independent columns.
A projection can have nonzero entries and still collapse a direction.
Zero determinant means the columns fail to form a basis. A projection such as $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ is nonzero but has dependent columns.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Zero determinant means the columns fail to form a basis. A projection such as $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ is nonzero but has dependent columns.

problems.promptMarkdown: A plane transformation scales one coordinate by $-2$ and the other by $3$. What is its signed area scale?

hints.bodyMarkdown: Distinguish signed scale from absolute area scale.
Multiply the two diagonal entries.
The negative factor records a reversal of orientation.
Its diagonal matrix has determinant $(-2)3=-6$. Areas grow by six, with orientation reversed.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Its diagonal matrix has determinant $(-2)3=-6$. Areas grow by six, with orientation reversed.

problems.promptMarkdown: If $B=P^{-1}AP$, how do the determinants compare?

hints.bodyMarkdown: Expand the determinant of the three factors.
Use multiplicativity and the determinant of an inverse.
The first and last determinant factors multiply to one.
Multiplicativity gives $\det B=\det(P^{-1})\det A\det P=\det A$. The change of coordinates cancels.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Multiplicativity gives $\det B=\det(P^{-1})\det A\det P=\det A$. The change of coordinates cancels.

problems.promptMarkdown: Prove that an invertible square matrix has nonzero determinant.

steps.textMarkdown: Take determinants and use multiplicativity: $\det A\det A^{-1}=\det I$.
Since $\det I=1$, the product on the left is nonzero.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Use the equation defining an inverse.
Determinants multiply under composition.
The identity determinant is one.
Apply the determinant to the inverse identity. A product equal to one cannot have a zero factor.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Apply the determinant to the inverse identity. A product equal to one cannot have a zero factor.
